notes: Safe with anyone at any time of day. Say it when you walk into a small shop or a lift: silence comes across as rude.

examples.tl: Hallo, heeft u een tafel voor twee?
examples.en: Hello, do you have a table for two?

notes: Casual and friendly, fine with people your own age and in most cafés. Also used for 'bye' among friends.
Until noon. The g is a soft scrape in the throat. Often clipped to 'Morgen!'

examples.en: Good morning, I have a reservation.

notes: From noon until about 6 pm. The standard opener with shop and museum staff.

examples.tl: Goedemiddag, twee kaartjes voor het museum, alstublieft.
examples.en: Good afternoon, two tickets for the museum, please.

notes: From about 6 pm. 'Goedenacht' and 'welterusten' are only for going to bed.

examples.tl: Goedenavond, we hebben gereserveerd voor zeven uur.
examples.en: Good evening, we have a reservation for seven o'clock.

notes: Works as hello and as goodbye. Leaving a shop you hear a drawn-out 'Daaag!'
Said 'doo-ee'. Cheerful and casual; cashiers and bartenders use it with everyone.
The polite goodbye for staff and strangers, literally 'until seeing'.

examples.tl: Dank u wel en tot ziens!

notes: Said by almost every cashier. In the evening: 'Fijne avond!' Answer with 'U ook!' or 'Jij ook!'

examples.tl: Alstublieft, uw bon. Fijne dag nog!
examples.en: Here you are, your receipt. Have a nice day!

notes: The reply to 'Fijne dag!', 'Fijn weekend!' and 'Eet smakelijk!'

examples.tl: Fijne avond! — Dank u, u ook!
examples.en: Have a nice evening! — Thank you, you too!

notes: Also said when handing something over: 'here you are'. Written a.u.b. on signs.
The 'wel' adds warmth, not meaning. With people your own age: 'dank je wel'.

examples.tl: Dank u wel voor uw hulp.

notes: Neutral: fits both u and je situations. 'Heel erg bedankt' = thanks very much.
Literally 'gladly done'. You will also hear 'geen dank' and plain 'alsjeblieft'.
The everyday apology, for bumping into someone or interrupting. For something serious: 'Het spijt me.'

examples.tl: Sorry, ik spreek niet zo goed Nederlands.
examples.en: Sorry, I don't speak Dutch very well.

notes: To get someone's attention or to get past. Stress on the second syllable: par-DON.

examples.tl: Pardon, is dit de tram naar Centraal Station?
examples.en: Excuse me, is this the tram to Central Station?

notes: Reply to 'sorry' or to a request. Also heard: 'geeft niks' (never mind).

examples.tl: Sorry, ik ben een beetje laat. — Geen probleem.
examples.en: Sorry, I'm a bit late. — No problem.

notes: Said 'yah'. 'Ja hoor' is a friendly 'sure'.
Said 'nay'. At Albert Heijn the cashier asks 'Heeft u een bonuskaart?': this is your answer.

examples.en: No, I don't have a loyalty card.

notes: The natural way to accept an offer. A bare 'ja' sounds a bit flat.

examples.tl: Wilt u er slagroom bij? — Ja, graag.
examples.en: Would you like whipped cream with it? — Yes, please.

notes: Careful: a bare 'dank u' in reply to an offer is usually taken as no. To accept, say 'ja, graag'.

examples.tl: Wilt u nog koffie? — Nee, dank u.
examples.en: Would you like more coffee? — No, thank you.

notes: After an order it means 'please': 'Een thee, graag.' With a verb it means 'like to': 'Ik wil graag...'
Used exactly as in English. 'Prima' = fine, great.

examples.tl: Oké, dan nemen we de volgende trein.
examples.en: Okay, then we'll take the next train.

notes: Said 'khoot'. Also the reply 'fine, okay': 'Is dat goed?' 'Ja, goed.'

examples.tl: Is morgen om tien uur goed?

notes: Said 'na-TUUR-luk'. A warm yes to a request.

examples.tl: Mag ik hier zitten? — Ja, natuurlijk.
examples.en: May I sit here? — Yes, of course.

notes: 'Ik snap het niet' is the casual version. 'Ik versta u niet' = I can't make out what you are saying.

examples.tl: Sorry, ik begrijp het niet. Kunt u het in het Engels zeggen?
examples.en: Sorry, I don't understand. Can you say it in English?

notes: Nearly everyone does and many switch as soon as they hear an accent. Opening in Dutch first is still seen as good manners.

examples.tl: Goedemiddag, spreekt u Engels? — Ja hoor, natuurlijk.
examples.en: Good afternoon, do you speak English? — Sure, of course.

notes: Languages are capitalized in Dutch: Nederlands, Engels.

examples.tl: Sorry, ik spreek geen Nederlands. Spreekt u Engels?
examples.en: Sorry, I don't speak Dutch. Do you speak English?

notes: Said 'un BAY-chuh'. Works for amounts and for degree: 'een beetje moe' = a bit tired.
A quick casual alternative is 'Sorry?' or 'Wat zegt u?' (what did you say?).

examples.tl: Sorry, kunt u dat herhalen? Ik verstond het niet.
examples.en: Sorry, can you repeat that? I didn't catch it.

accept: Can you speak a bit slower?
notes: Langzaam = slow, langzamer = slower. 'Wat' here means 'a bit'.

examples.tl: Kunt u wat langzamer praten, alstublieft? Ik leer Nederlands.
examples.en: Can you speak a bit more slowly, please? I'm learning Dutch.

notes: Point at the word on a menu or sign while you ask.

examples.tl: Wat betekent dit woord op de menukaart?
examples.en: What does this word on the menu mean?

notes: The verb after 'ik' is the bare stem: ik ben, ik heb, ik wil, ik ga.
For staff, strangers and older people; the verb ends in -t (u bent, u heeft). Staff often say 'je' to you: normal, not rude.
'Jij' is the stressed form. Use it with people your own age in bars, hostels and at a race. Plural 'you all' = jullie.
'Dit' for het-words and for pointing at anything; 'deze' before de-words: deze trein, dit station.
'Dat' for het-words and for pointing; 'die' before de-words: die tram, dat huis.
Said like English 'here'. Opposite: daar (there).

examples.tl: Ik ben hier voor de marathon.

notes: Said like the letter N. Not to be confused with 'een' (a / one).

examples.tl: Een koffie en een appeltaart, alstublieft.
examples.en: A coffee and an apple pie, please.

notes: Trap: Dutch 'of' is English 'or'. English 'of' is 'van'.
Comes after the verb and its object: 'Ik weet het niet.' Before a noun with no article, use 'geen' instead.
Also 'by' for transport: met de trein, met de fiets.
Handy for orders: zonder suiker (no sugar), zonder ui (no onion), zonder vlees (no meat).

examples.tl: Een broodje kaas zonder boter, alstublieft.
examples.en: A cheese sandwich without butter, please.

notes: Also 'some / a bit': 'wat water' = some water.

examples.en: What would you like to drink?

notes: Said to you by staff, or by you while you dig for your ticket or card.

examples.tl: Een momentje, alstublieft, ik zoek mijn kaartje.
examples.en: One moment, please, I'm looking for my ticket.

notes: Polite way to address a man you do not know. Said 'muh-NAYR'. To a group: 'heren'.

examples.tl: Pardon, meneer, u vergeet uw tas.
examples.en: Excuse me, sir, you're forgetting your bag.

notes: For any adult woman, married or not. Said 'muh-VROW'. To a group: 'dames'.
